title: Hume
orientation: Russell presents David Hume (1711-76) as the philosopher who pushed Locke's and Berkeley's empiricism to its logical conclusion and, in doing so, made it self-consistent but 'incredible' -- a philosophical 'dead end' from which, Russell says, 'it is impossible to go further.' The chapter reconstructs Hume's distinction between impressions and ideas, his dissolution of the self into a 'bundle of perceptions,' and above all his devastating analysis of causation and induction, before Russell offers his own assessment of exactly how much of Hume's scepticism can, and cannot, be answered.
historical_background: Hume wrote his major philosophical work, the Treatise of Human Nature, while living in France between 1734 and 1737; published in 1739-40 while he was still in his twenties, it 'fell dead-born from the press,' attracting no attention at all. He later condensed it (omitting its best arguments) into the more successful Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding -- the book that famously awakened Kant from his 'dogmatic slumbers,' though Kant seems never to have read the original Treatise. Hume also wrote Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (published posthumously, 1779), an Essay on Miracles, and a History of England; he visited Paris in 1763, was feted by the philosophes, and had a notorious falling-out with the paranoid Rousseau, in which, Russell notes, 'Hume behaved with admirable forbearance.'
philosophical_problems: What is the correct distinction between 'impressions' (vivid, original perceptions) and 'ideas' (fainter copies of impressions), and does all thought reduce to copies of prior sense-experience?
Is there a genuine, unified 'self' or 'soul' underlying our experiences, or is the self merely a bundle of perceptions with no substance behind it?
What do we actually mean when we say 'A causes B,' and can causal necessity be perceived, or only constant conjunction?
Is there any rational justification for inductive inference -- for expecting the future to resemble the past -- or is such expectation merely a product of habit and custom?
If reason cannot justify our most basic beliefs (in causation, in an external world, in our own continued existence), what, if anything, legitimately grounds belief and action?

philosophers_discussed.name: David Hume
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject: Russell reconstructs his theory of impressions and ideas, his critique of the self, his revolutionary and sceptical analysis of causation and induction, and his ultimate retreat into 'natural credulity' and 'carelessness and inattention' as the only practical antidotes to total scepticism.

philosophers_discussed.name: George Berkeley
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as the source of the nominalist doctrine of abstract ideas that Hume explicitly and emphatically endorses at the opening of his own discussion of abstraction.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Identified as the philosophical starting point Hume shares -- 'like Locke, [Hume begins] with the intention of being sensible and empirical' -- but whom Hume surpasses in rigor, arriving at conclusions Locke's 'comfortable inconsistencies' allowed him to avoid.

philosophers_discussed.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the philosopher whom Hume's Enquiry (not, apparently, the Treatise) 'awakened ... from his dogmatic slumbers'; Russell nonetheless argues Kant and his followers remained, in substance, pre-Humian rationalists who can themselves be refuted by Humian arguments.

philosophers_discussed.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Discussed in connection with his quarrel with Hume, and, more importantly, as symbolizing (alongside Hume) the 'great outburst of irrational faith' that followed the collapse of eighteenth-century rationalism into Humian scepticism -- Rousseau agreed no belief is based on reason but elevated 'the heart' over reason instead.

philosophers_discussed.name: Henri Bergson
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as sharing, with 'almost all philosophers down to and including' him, the mistaken assumption that causal laws take the simple form 'A causes B,' a form Russell says 'do[es] not occur in any well-developed science.'

core_concepts.name: Impressions and ideas
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Hume divides all mental contents ('perceptions') into two kinds: 'impressions,' the vivid, forceful experiences of direct sensation or feeling, and 'ideas,' the fainter copies or images of those impressions that occur in thinking and remembering. Complex ideas (like a 'winged horse') can combine simple ideas in new ways, but every simple idea must ultimately trace back to a corresponding simple impression.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hume's foundational distinction: impressions 'have more force and violence,' while 'by ideas I mean the faint images of these in thinking and reasoning'; his key principle is that 'every simple idea has a simple impression, which resembles it; and every simple impression a correspondent idea,' with complex ideas (which need not resemble any single impression) built out of simple ones.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This distinction is the foundation of Hume's entire epistemology and his most famous methodological maxim -- 'no idea without an antecedent impression' -- inherited from Locke but stated with far greater rigor and consistency.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Opens Book I of the Treatise of Human Nature (1739).
examples: A man born blind has no idea of colours, since he has never had the corresponding impressions
We can imagine a winged horse (a complex idea) despite never perceiving one, because its components (wings, horse) are each drawn from real impressions
objections: Russell's psychological objection: Hume ignores vagueness -- a recalled image of a specific shade of colour or a specific height is rarely precise enough to distinguish it from very similar shades or heights, contrary to Hume's claim that ideas 'exactly represent' their impressions
This vagueness explains, contra Hume's own difficulty, how we might imagine an intermediate shade of colour between two similar shades we have actually seen
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became the central axiom of the entire empiricist tradition following Hume.

core_concepts.name: The dissolution of the Self into a 'bundle of perceptions'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Hume looked inward for some core 'self' beneath all his thoughts and feelings, and found nothing: only a constantly changing stream of particular perceptions (a sight, a sound, a feeling of pain) with no separate 'self' holding them together. He concluded the mind is really just a bundle of these perceptions, not a distinct thing that has them.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hume denies any impression, and therefore any idea, of the self: 'when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other ... I never catch myself at any time without a perception'; he concludes we are 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell regards this as 'of great importance' and largely correct: it eliminates the last surviving philosophical use of 'substance' from psychology (as Berkeley had eliminated it from physics), undermines theological claims to knowledge of an immortal 'soul,' and shows the subject/object distinction is not epistemologically fundamental.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book I, Part IV, Section VI of the Treatise ('Of Personal Identity').
examples: Hume's introspective search, finding only 'heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure' but never a bare 'self' apart from these
competing_positions: The traditional (Cartesian/scholastic) doctrine of the self as a persisting mental substance
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell endorses the core logical point -- that ideas of unperceived things (like the self, or one's own brain) can be defined in terms of perceived things, so nothing need be added beyond the bundle of perceptions -- as something 'any thoroughgoing empiricist must agree with.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly undermines theological claims to 'supposed knowledge of the soul.'

core_concepts.name: The analysis of causation: constant conjunction, not necessary connection
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Hume argued we never actually perceive one event 'making' another happen -- we only ever observe that events of one kind (A) are regularly followed by events of another kind (B). We never see the hidden 'power' or 'necessity' supposedly connecting them; that feeling of necessity is really just a habit our minds form after repeatedly observing the two events together.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hume's objective claim: 'we have no other notion of cause and effect, but that of certain objects, which have been always conjoined together ... we cannot penetrate into the reason of the conjunction'; causation reduces to constant, observed conjunction (or immediate succession) between event-types, not any further, perceivable 'necessary connection.' His subjective claim: this felt sense of necessity arises because 'custom operating upon the imagination' -- the frequent past conjunction of A and B causes the impression of A to produce a vivid, belief-constituting idea of B.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this 'the first really serious challenge' to the traditional (Cartesian/scholastic) assimilation of causal connection to logical, necessary connection, and says 'the modern philosophy of causation begins' with Hume; Russell judges the objective half of the doctrine essentially correct, especially regarding physics, where simple 'A causes B' laws never actually survive in well-developed science.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book I, Part III of the Treatise, especially the sections 'Of Knowledge and Probability' and the discussion of the idea of necessary connection.
examples: Hume's example of two perfectly accurate chronometers striking the hours one after another invariably, without either causing the other's striking, used by Hume's opponents to argue constant conjunction alone cannot be all there is to causation
objections: Russell's opponents-of-Hume argument: some relations (e.g., between a volition and the resulting bodily movement) might be directly perceived as more than mere sequence -- though Russell notes physiology (nerve and muscle processes between will and movement) makes this doubtful
Russell notes it is 'rash to suppose that we perceive causal relations when we think we do,' tilting the balance, on this narrower point, toward Hume
competing_positions: The traditional Cartesian/scholastic view that causal connections are logically necessary, akin to relations of ground and consequent
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes 'almost all philosophers down to and including Bergson' inherited Hume's simplified 'A causes B' model of causal laws, a model Russell says does not actually match how mature sciences formulate causal laws.

core_concepts.name: The problem of induction
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Even if we've seen event A followed by event B a thousand times before, Hume argues, nothing guarantees it will happen the same way next time. We can't prove this using logic (since we can at least imagine nature changing), and we can't prove it using past experience either, because that would be circular -- using the very kind of reasoning (induction) that's in question to justify induction itself.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hume's sceptical argument: any rational justification for expecting future conjunctions to resemble past ones would require the principle 'that instances of which we have had no experience resemble those of which we have had experience'; this principle is not logically necessary (a change in nature's course is conceivable) and cannot be established by any 'probable' (i.e., empirical) argument either, since all such arguments already presuppose it -- so 'the supposition that the future resembles the past is ... derived entirely from habit,' not reason.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell regards this as Hume's single most important and, in a precise sense, unanswerable result: 'What these arguments prove -- and I do not think the proof can be controverted -- is that induction is an independent logical principle, incapable of being inferred either from experience or from other logical principles, and that without this principle science is impossible.' This makes empiricism alone insufficient as a foundation for science.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book I, Part III, Sections IV, VI, and VIII of the Treatise.
examples: The apple example: past experience leads me to expect an apple will taste like an apple, not like roast beef, but Hume argues this expectation has, strictly, 'not a shadow of a reason' behind it beyond habit
The expectation that the sun will rise tomorrow, which Russell notes has, on Hume's principles, no more rational grounding than any other habitual expectation
objections: Russell's internal-consistency objection: if the objective half of Hume's causal doctrine is right, then even psychological habit-formation (which is itself a causal process) gives no genuine reason to expect habits to continue forming the same way in future, so Hume's own appeal to 'the law of habit' as an explanation is not obviously available to him on his own terms
competing_positions: Empiricists who accept Hume's rejection of necessary connection but reject his rejection of induction by simple enumeration, holding that sufficiently numerous past conjunctions do raise the probability of future ones
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell states this 'challenge to philosophers ... has still not been adequately met,' framing the problem of induction as one of the central unsolved problems of subsequent philosophy of science.

core_concepts.name: Hume's total scepticism and his retreat into 'natural credulity'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Having argued that no belief -- not even belief in cause and effect, an external world, or the continuity of the self -- can be rationally justified, Hume doesn't conclude we should stop believing these things. Instead, he says nature simply forces us to believe them anyway, whether or not reason can back them up; the only 'remedy' for his own sceptical doubts is 'carelessness and inattention.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hume concludes 'all probable reasoning is nothing but a species of sensation,' and that belief is 'more properly an act of the sensitive, than of the cogitative part of our natures'; he does not refute his own sceptical arguments but instead falls back on the claim that 'nature, by an absolute and uncontrollable necessity has determined us to judge as well as to breathe and feel,' recommending 'carelessness and inattention' as the only practical remedy for total scepticism.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as 'the bankruptcy of eighteenth-century reasonableness': Hume set out, in the spirit of Locke, to be purely sensible and empirical, but his superior rigor led him to the 'disastrous conclusion that from experience and observation nothing is to be learnt' -- and Russell judges Hume's practical abandonment of his own scepticism to be, in a sense, 'insincere,' since he cannot actually live by it.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Book I, Part IV, Sections I and II of the Treatise ('Of scepticism with regard to reason' and 'Of scepticism with regard to the senses').
examples: Hume's own 'funeral oration' describing his mild, cheerful temperament, which Russell contrasts with the destructive implications of his philosophy
Hume's admission that he continues to believe fire warms and water refreshes only because 'it costs us too much pains to think otherwise'
objections: Russell's charge of inconsistency: in the later, non-sceptical portions of the Treatise, Hume 'forgets all about his fundamental doubts' and writes like any other Enlightenment moralist, applying to himself the very 'carelessness and inattention' he elsewhere prescribes as a philosophical remedy

Russell notes Hume has no right, on his own principles, to call anything 'dangerous' (a causal word) once he has undermined rational belief in causation, yet Hume does call the errors of religion 'dangerous'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell argues this self-refutation of Enlightenment rationality was 'inevitably ... followed by a great outburst of irrational faith,' symbolized by Hume's quarrel with the emotionally volatile Rousseau, and feeding into nineteenth- and twentieth-century currents of 'unreason.'

arguments.title: The argument for the bundle theory of the self
premises: All our ideas must be derived from corresponding impressions (Hume's foundational empiricist principle).
Introspecting carefully, one never encounters an impression of a bare 'self' -- only particular perceptions (a sensation, an emotion, a thought).
Since there is no impression of the self, there can be no genuine idea of the self as a distinct, unified thing.
arguments.conclusion: The self is nothing more than 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions,' in constant flux, not a persisting mental substance.
arguments.explanation: Russell largely endorses this argument's logical structure, noting that ideas of unperceived things (like one's own brain, or the self) can always in principle be defined in terms of perceived things, so that 'all psychological knowledge can be stated without introducing the \"Self.\"'
objections: It does not follow, Russell notes, that there is no simple self -- only that we cannot know whether there is one, since it could never itself be perceived and thus could never enter into empirical knowledge
implications: Removes the last philosophical use of 'substance' from psychology, following Berkeley's earlier removal of substance from physics
Undermines theological claims to knowledge of an immortal soul

arguments.title: The argument that causation is nothing but constant conjunction
premises: The power by which one event supposedly produces another cannot be discovered merely by examining the ideas of the two events in themselves.
We can only come to expect B from A through repeated experience of A and B occurring together (constant conjunction), never through pure reasoning about a single instance.
Nothing in this experience reveals anything beyond the fact of regular conjunction or succession -- no further, perceivable 'necessary connection' is ever given.
arguments.conclusion: When we say 'A causes B,' all we are entitled to mean is that events of type A have, in past experience, been constantly conjoined with events of type B; there is no additional, perceivable necessity binding them.
arguments.explanation: Russell judges the 'objective' half of this doctrine essentially correct, especially for physics, where 'simple rules of the form \"A causes B\" are never to be admitted ... except as crude suggestions in early stages,' being replaced by causal laws far too complex to be given directly in perception.
objections: Opponents argue some relations (e.g., volition and bodily movement) might be directly perceived as more than mere succession -- though physiological complexity (the long causal chain of nerve and muscle processes) makes this doubtful, per Russell
implications: Undermines any account of scientific law as expressing logically necessary connections
Sets up Hume's further, more radical argument that even constant conjunction gives no rational ground for future expectation (the problem of induction)

arguments.title: The problem of induction (the argument from the impossibility of justifying the uniformity of nature)
premises: Any justification for expecting the future to resemble the past would require assuming the principle that unexperienced instances resemble experienced ones (the uniformity of nature).
This principle cannot be a logically necessary truth, since a change in the course of nature is conceivable without contradiction.

The principle also cannot be established by any 'probable' (empirical) argument, since every probable argument already presupposes the very principle in question -- making any such justification viciously circular.
arguments.conclusion: There is no rational justification for inductive inference; our confidence that the future will resemble the past 'is derived entirely from habit,' not from reason.
arguments.explanation: Russell treats this as Hume's deepest and, in his judgment, unrefuted result, concluding that 'induction is an independent logical principle, incapable of being inferred either from experience or from other logical principles, and that without this principle science is impossible' -- meaning pure empiricism alone cannot ground science; some further, non-empirical principle must be assumed.
objections: Russell notes that if taken fully seriously, this argument makes 'all expectation as to the future irrational, even the expectation that we shall continue to feel expectations,' including expectation that the sun will rise tomorrow
implications: Reveals a fundamental limitation in pure empiricism as a foundation for scientific knowledge
Frames the central task Russell sets for post-Humian epistemology: finding some defensible, non-empirical principle of induction

arguments.title: Russell's internal critique of Hume's psychological explanation of belief
premises: Hume explains our belief in future conjunctions (e.g., that an apple will taste like an apple) as caused by habitual association from past constant conjunction, not by rational justification.
But 'the law of habit' -- that repeated past conjunctions cause present expectations -- is itself a causal generalization.

By Hume's own objective doctrine of causation, no past conjunction (including conjunctions between experience and habit-formation) gives any rational ground for expecting the same conjunction to hold in the future.
arguments.conclusion: Hume is not entitled, by his own principles, to assume that the law of habit will itself continue to operate reliably in the future -- his psychological explanation of belief covertly relies on exactly the kind of causal, inductive assumption his scepticism was meant to undermine.
arguments.explanation: Russell illustrates this with a deliberately absurd extension of Hume's own logic: 'perhaps the next time I see an apple I shall expect it to taste like roast beef' -- since nothing in Hume's system guarantees that even our habits of expectation will remain stable over time.
implications: Shows that Hume's retreat to psychological explanation does not actually escape his own scepticism, but merely relocates the same unresolved problem one level up

key_distinctions: Relations depending only on ideas (yielding certainty) vs. relations that can change without any change in ideas (yielding only probability)
The 'objective' half of Hume's causal doctrine (no necessary connection, only conjunction) vs. the 'subjective' half (belief as habit-caused expectation)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Hume explicitly endorses Berkeley's nominalist doctrine of abstract general ideas at the outset of his discussion of abstraction; he inherits and radicalizes Locke's maxim 'no idea without an antecedent impression,' pursuing Locke's empiricism with a rigor and consistency that, per Russell, Locke's own 'comfortable inconsistencies' had allowed him to avoid, and thereby exposing (rather than resolving) the very problem -- how ideas relate to a mind-independent world -- that Russell had identified as Locke's central unresolved difficulty.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Hume's Enquiry famously 'awakened Kant from his dogmatic slumbers,' though Russell disputes that Kant's Critique of Pure Reason genuinely answers Hume, arguing Kant and Hegel represent 'a pre-Humian type of rationalism' still refutable by Humian arguments; Russell also credits Hume with beginning 'the modern philosophy of causation,' a line running forward through subsequent empiricist philosophy of science, and frames the unresolved problem of induction as a live challenge for that entire later tradition.
political_social_context: Russell notes Hume was a Tory whose History of England argued for the superiority of Tories to Whigs and Scotchmen to Englishmen, and briefly connects the collapse of Humian rational empiricism to a broader 'growth of unreason throughout the nineteenth century and what has passed of the twentieth,' symbolized by Hume's own quarrel with Rousseau -- 'Rousseau was mad but influential, Hume was sane but had no followers.'
religion_science_culture_context: Hume's Essay on Miracles argued there can never be adequate historical evidence for miraculous events, and his posthumously published Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion extended his scepticism to natural theology; Russell frames Hume's overall philosophical trajectory as 'the bankruptcy of eighteenth-century reasonableness,' with far-reaching implications for the status of scientific, as well as religious, knowledge.
russell_presentation: Russell treats Hume with unusual respect combined with real alarm: Hume is 'one of the most important among philosophers' precisely because, by reasoning more rigorously and consistently than Locke or Berkeley, he pushed empiricism to conclusions that are 'equally difficult to refute and to accept.' Russell reconstructs Hume's system in stages -- the impressions/ideas distinction, the bundle theory of the self, and finally the analysis of causation and induction -- reserving his most sustained engagement for the latter, which he calls 'the most important part of the whole Treatise.' Russell endorses much of Hume's 'objective' doctrine of causation (that causal laws, properly stated, involve nothing beyond conjunction) while pressing Hume on an internal inconsistency: Hume's own psychological explanation of belief (the 'law of habit') is itself a causal claim that his scepticism about induction should, if taken seriously, equally undermine. Russell treats the problem of induction as Hume's deepest and still-unanswered achievement -- 'a challenge to philosophers, which, in my opinion, has still not been adequately met' -- and closes by arguing that Hume's own retreat into 'natural credulity' and 'carelessness and inattention' is a practical, not a philosophical, solution: sincere as psychology, but an admission of intellectual defeat. Russell's own tentative way forward is to isolate the principle of induction as an independent, non-empirical logical principle that any workable science must simply assume, since it 'cannot, without circularity, be inferred from observed uniformities.'
critical_context: Common scholarly assessment, largely shared by Russell: subsequent philosophers (Kant among them) have repeatedly claimed to 'refute' Hume, but Russell states plainly that he finds 'none of their refutations convincing.' Later development: the problem of induction Hume raises remains, in the history and philosophy of science, one of the most persistently debated unresolved problems, with responses ranging from Kantian synthetic a priori principles, to Popperian falsificationism (which reframes rather than solves the justification problem), to various probabilistic and pragmatic treatments -- none of which, in Russell's own assessment as he writes this chapter, had settled the matter.
key_takeaways: Hume distinguishes vivid 'impressions' from fainter, derivative 'ideas,' holding that every simple idea must trace back to a corresponding simple impression.
Hume dissolves the self into 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions,' finding no impression, and therefore no idea, of a persisting mental substance.

Hume's analysis of causation holds that we never perceive necessary connection between cause and effect, only constant conjunction or succession -- a view Russell regards as 'the first really serious challenge' to earlier, logically-necessitarian theories of causation.

Hume's problem of induction shows that no rational justification -- neither logical nor empirical -- can be given for expecting the future to resemble the past, a result Russell calls unrefuted and fundamental to the limits of pure empiricism.

Confronted with his own total scepticism, Hume does not refute it but instead appeals to 'natural credulity' and recommends 'carelessness and inattention' as the only practical remedy -- a move Russell judges intellectually honest but philosophically unsatisfying and, in practice, 'insincere.'
Russell argues Hume's own psychological explanation of belief (via habit) covertly relies on the same kind of causal assumption his scepticism about induction undermines.
Russell treats Hume's philosophy as a 'dead end' for empiricism -- consistent but incredible -- that later rationalists (including Kant) have not genuinely refuted, only side-stepped.
study_notes:
This is the capstone chapter of Russell's three-chapter arc on Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, and it is worth reading it explicitly as a culmination: Locke's empiricism harbored an unresolved inconsistency about how ideas connect to an external world; Berkeley tried to dissolve that problem by denying matter altogether, at the cost of resting everything on God's perpetual perception; Hume, more rigorous than either, refuses Berkeley's theological shortcut and instead follows empiricist principles all the way down -- with the result that even causation, the external world, and the self dissolve into mere habitual, unjustified belief.

The chapter's structural backbone is the move from the impressions/ideas distinction, through the bundle theory of self, to the analysis of causation, and finally to the problem of induction -- each step more radical and more destructive than the last. Pay special attention to Russell's own two-part decomposition of Hume's causal doctrine into an 'objective' claim (causation is just constant conjunction) and a 'subjective' claim (belief in causation is just habitual association) -- and to Russell's sharp internal objection that the subjective claim quietly smuggles back in the very kind of causal assumption ('the law of habit will continue') that Hume's argument about induction says cannot be rationally justified.

Finally, notice how Russell frames Hume's philosophy in terms of a stark trade-off between consistency and credibility (a theme first raised in the Locke chapters): Hume achieves near-total consistency, but at the cost of conclusions no one, including Hume himself in ordinary life, can actually believe. Russell's own closing assessment -- that the problem of induction is real, serious, and still unsolved -- should be read as his invitation to the reader to see this not as a historical curiosity but as an open problem in the philosophy of science.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A vivid, direct experience -- like actually seeing red or feeling pain -- as opposed to just imagining or remembering it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's term for perceptions with 'more force and violence,' the original, direct data of sensation and feeling from which all simple ideas are copied.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A fainter, copied version of an impression -- like remembering or imagining red, rather than actually seeing it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's term for the 'faint images' of impressions occurring in thinking, reasoning, memory, and imagination; simple ideas must resemble a corresponding simple impression.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that there is no single 'self' behind our thoughts and feelings -- just a constantly changing collection of individual perceptions.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's conclusion, from the absence of any impression of the self, that personal identity consists in nothing but 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions ... in a perpetual flux and movement.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The simple fact that one kind of event has always, so far, been followed by another kind of event -- which, for Hume, is all that 'causation' really amounts to.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's reductive account of causation: the observed regularity of one type of event being followed or accompanied by another, without any further perceivable necessary connection.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The puzzle of why we're justified in assuming the future will be like the past, given that we can't prove this using either pure logic or past experience (without going in a circle).
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's demonstration that the principle of the uniformity of nature -- required to justify inductive inference from observed to unobserved cases -- can be established neither a priori nor by any non-circular empirical argument.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Hume's term for the fact that, whatever philosophy proves or fails to prove, human nature simply forces us to go on believing in cause and effect, an external world, and so on.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Hume's appeal, in the face of his own total scepticism, to an unavoidable, non-rational psychological disposition ('nature ... has determined us to judge') that sustains ordinary belief despite the absence of rational justification.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Hume draw between 'impressions' and 'ideas'?
questions.answer: Impressions are vivid, forceful perceptions (direct sensation or feeling); ideas are fainter copies or images of impressions occurring in thinking, reasoning, memory, and imagination. Every simple idea must correspond to, and resemble, a prior simple impression.
questions.explanation: This distinction opens Book I of the Treatise and underlies Hume's entire epistemology.

questions.prompt: What does Hume conclude about the existence of a unified 'self' after introspecting on his own experience?
questions.answer: That there is no impression, and therefore no idea, of a unified self; introspection reveals only particular perceptions (sensations, feelings, thoughts) in constant flux, so the self is 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions.'
questions.explanation: This is Hume's famous 'bundle theory' of personal identity, which Russell regards as largely correct.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher's Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding is said to have 'awakened' another famous philosopher 'from his dogmatic slumbers'?
questions.explanation: Russell notes it was apparently the Enquiry, not the earlier and more thorough Treatise, that had this effect on Kant, since Kant does not appear to have known the Treatise.

questions.prompt: Contrast Hume's 'objective' and 'subjective' claims about causation.
questions.answer: The objective claim: when we say 'A causes B,' all we are entitled to mean is that A and B have been constantly conjoined in past experience, with no further perceivable necessary connection. The subjective claim: our belief that A and B are causally connected arises because repeated past conjunction of impressions of A with ideas of B, through habit, produces a vivid, belief-constituting idea of B whenever we perceive A.
questions.explanation: Russell treats the objective claim as largely correct but shows the subjective claim covertly relies on the very kind of causal assumption Hume's scepticism about induction calls into question.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Hume's argument that there is no rational justification for inductive inference.
questions.answer: Any rational justification for expecting the future to resemble the past would require the principle that unexperienced instances resemble experienced ones. This principle is not logically necessary (a change in nature's course is conceivable). It also cannot be established by any empirical/probable argument, since every such argument already presupposes the very principle in question. Therefore there is no non-circular rational justification for induction; our expectation of resemblance is 'derived entirely from habit.'
questions.explanation: Russell calls this Hume's deepest and, in his own judgment, unrefuted result.

questions.prompt: How does Hume respond, in practice, to the total scepticism his own arguments seem to generate?
questions.answer: He does not refute the sceptical arguments but appeals to 'natural credulity' -- nature forces us to judge and believe regardless of whether reason can justify it -- and recommends 'carelessness and inattention' as the only workable remedy for sceptical doubt.
questions.explanation: Russell reads this as an honest but philosophically unsatisfying retreat, and notes Hume cannot actually sustain his scepticism in the later, non-sceptical portions of the Treatise.

questions.prompt: How does Russell's assessment of Hume differ from Kant's self-understanding regarding the relationship between their two philosophies?
questions.answer: Kant believed his Critique of Pure Reason successfully answered Hume's scepticism. Russell disagrees, arguing Kant (and Hegel after him) represent 'a pre-Humian type of rationalism' that can itself be refuted by Humian arguments, and that only thinkers who do not pretend to be rational (like Rousseau, Schopenhauer, and Nietzsche) escape Hume's challenge -- though at the cost of abandoning rationality altogether.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's more provocative historiographical claims in the chapter.

flashcards.front: What are Hume's two kinds of 'perceptions'?
flashcards.back: Impressions (vivid, forceful direct experiences) and ideas (fainter copies of impressions).

flashcards.front: What is Hume's maxim about ideas and impressions?
flashcards.back: 'No idea without an antecedent impression': every simple idea must correspond to and resemble a prior simple impression.

flashcards.front: What does Hume conclude the 'self' actually is?
flashcards.back: A bundle or collection of different perceptions in constant flux -- not a persisting mental substance.

flashcards.front: What book of Hume's 'fell dead-born from the press'?
What later, more successful book did Hume condense the Treatise into?
Which philosopher did Hume's Enquiry famously 'awaken ... from his dogmatic slumbers'?
What is Hume's 'objective' doctrine of causation?
flashcards.back: Causation is nothing more than constant conjunction (or immediate succession) between event-types; there is no perceivable necessary connection.

flashcards.front: What is Hume's explanation for our felt sense of causal necessity?
flashcards.back: It arises from custom/habit: repeated observed conjunction of A and B causes the impression of A to produce a vivid, belief-constituting idea of B.
The question of what, if anything, rationally justifies expecting the future to resemble the past -- which Hume argues cannot be justified either logically or empirically without circularity.

flashcards.front: What does Hume conclude the belief that fire warms is ultimately based on?
flashcards.back: Habit -- 'it costs us too much pains to think otherwise,' not rational justification.

flashcards.front: What practical 'remedy' does Hume propose for total philosophical scepticism?
What does Russell call Hume's philosophy, in terms of the empiricist tradition?
flashcards.back: A 'dead end' -- consistent but incredible; 'in his direction, it is impossible to go further.'

flashcards.front: What is Russell's internal objection to Hume's 'law of habit' explanation of belief?
flashcards.back: The law of habit is itself a causal claim, so Hume's own scepticism about induction should equally undermine his confidence that habits will keep forming the same way in future.

flashcards.front: Whom did Hume famously quarrel with in Paris in 1763?

quiz.prompt: According to Hume, what is the key difference between an 'impression' and an 'idea'?
options: Impressions are always false, ideas are always true
Impressions have more force and vividness; ideas are fainter copies of them
quiz.explanation: Hume defines impressions as the vivid, forceful originals and ideas as their fainter mental copies.

quiz.prompt: What does Hume conclude the 'self' really is?
options: A bundle of different perceptions in constant flux
A material substance in the brain
quiz.explanation: Hume's introspection reveals no impression of a unified self, leading him to the bundle theory.
quiz.related_concept: The dissolution of the Self into a 'bundle of perceptions'

quiz.prompt: True or False: Hume's Treatise of Human Nature was an immediate popular success when first published.
quiz.explanation: Hume himself said it 'fell dead-born from the press,' attracting almost no attention.

quiz.prompt: According to Hume's 'objective' doctrine of causation, what does 'A causes B' actually mean?
options: A and B have been constantly conjoined in past experience
A is morally superior to B
A and B share a common substance
quiz.explanation: Hume reduces causal claims to observed constant conjunction, denying any further perceivable necessary connection.
quiz.related_concept: The analysis of causation: constant conjunction, not necessary connection

quiz.prompt: What does Hume's problem of induction show, according to Russell?
options: That induction cannot be rationally justified by either logic or (non-circular) experience
That all scientific laws are false
That Locke's philosophy was entirely correct
quiz.explanation: Russell treats this as Hume's deepest result: no non-circular justification for induction is available.

quiz.prompt: Hume's proposed remedy for total philosophical scepticism is ____ and inattention.
quiz.explanation: Hume recommends 'carelessness and inattention' as the only practical antidote to inescapable sceptical doubt.
quiz.related_concept: Hume's total scepticism and his retreat into 'natural credulity'

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's internal objection to Hume's psychological ('law of habit') explanation of belief in causation?
options: It is itself a causal claim that Hume's own scepticism about induction should undermine
It was never actually stated by Hume
quiz.explanation: Russell points out the 'law of habit' is itself causal, so Hume's argument against rationally justified induction applies to it as much as to any other causal belief.
quiz.related_concept: Hume's total scepticism and his retreat into 'natural credulity'

quiz.prompt: True or False: Russell believes Kant's Critique of Pure Reason successfully refutes Hume's scepticism.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues Kant and his followers represent a 'pre-Humian type of rationalism' still vulnerable to Humian arguments, rather than a genuine refutation of Hume.
quiz.related_concept: The analysis of causation: constant conjunction, not necessary connection

quiz.prompt: Match each claim to its type in Hume's causal doctrine: (1) 'A and B have been constantly conjoined,' (2) 'Repeated conjunction causes us, by habit, to expect B upon perceiving A.'
options: (1) Both are objective; (2) Both are subjective
(1) Neither is part of Hume's doctrine; (2) Neither is part of Hume's doctrine
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly divides Hume's causal doctrine into an objective half (about conjunction) and a subjective half (about the psychological origin of belief).
quiz.related_concept: The analysis of causation: constant conjunction, not necessary connection

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Hume's argument that the self is merely 'a bundle of perceptions.' Does Russell's endorsement of this argument's logical structure commit him to denying that a persisting self could exist?
rubric: Clear statement of Russell's qualified endorsement
Discussion of what the argument does and does not prove

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's claim that Hume's problem of induction 'has still not been adequately met.' Present and assess at least one possible response to Hume's argument (from Hume's own text, from Kant, or from your own reasoning).
rubric: Accurate statement of the problem of induction
Clear presentation of at least one proposed response
Critical assessment of that response's adequacy

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Hume's total philosophical scepticism with his practical, everyday conduct as described by Russell (his cheerful temperament, his ordinary beliefs). What does this contrast suggest about the relationship between philosophical argument and lived belief?
rubric: Accurate account of Hume's practical retreat into natural credulity
Discussion of the tension Russell identifies
